promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Nov 1 2026, 5 weeks out, target under 3:45.

new.headline: You followed last week's plan exactly, so this week steps up modestly to 44 miles. Doubling to 80 would put the marathon at risk, and it would not make you fitter in time.

answers.question: My club mate runs 70 miles a week before a marathon. I'm thinking of doubling to 80 next week to catch up, running twice a day. Would that work?
answers.answer:
No, I would not double to 80 miles next week, and I would not add a second run each day.

Going from 40 to 80 doubles your load in one step. Two weeks ago you jumped from 37 to 53 miles, a rise of 43 percent, and your calves were tight that Sunday night. Your legs were heavy early last week.

You cannot catch up in five weeks. Fitness from a big week shows up weeks later, but the cost of overdoing it shows up within days. An injury now would end the build.

Your club mate built to 70 over a long time, while you were at about 30 miles a week before this build. Your two rest days are also where you adapt, so keep them.

The plan steps you up to 44 miles this week and keeps building in small steps toward the high 40s before the taper. Marathon-pace work and long runs will get you under 3:45, not the weekly total.

new.analysis:
Last week went exactly to the plan, and that matters more than any single number. Every run matched its planned distance, the rest days stayed rest days, and the marathon-pace miles landed between 8:30 and 8:40 against the 8:35 you need for 3:45. The week of Sep 7 – 13 was the opposite, with an extra run, a fourth rep and a 20-mile long run.

The recent weekly miles explain why this week rises only a little. You went 37, then 53, then 40, so last week worked as the lighter week after a big jump. Moving to 44 puts you above last week without returning to the load that left your legs heavy.

The long run is where the plan is most deliberate. You have already run 3h20 at 20 miles, which is beyond the 2.5 to 3 hours I want from the key session, so going longer gains little. What you need now is another solid, controlled long run. If this one goes cleanly, I expect to add marathon-pace segments to the next one.

An easy-running share in the low 60s is expected on a week with a marathon-pace session. The warm-up, cool-down and the pace miles themselves count as harder time. The long run is the only place where a slower start would raise that share without costing you anything.

Thursday is longer than your usual easy day on purpose. A marathon rewards a medium-long run during the week. Running it easy the day after the quality session adds endurance without a second hard day.
